title: Alchemy and the Great Work — what they actually did
desc: What alchemists did in the laboratory, what they thought they were doing, and why the argument about spiritual versus chemical alchemy is still open.
tldr: Alchemy is where the Hermetic scheme meets a furnace. Practitioners spent decades on real operations with real glassware, described in deliberately impossible language, aiming at a result they called the Great Work. Whether they also meant a transformation of themselves is the field's longest-running argument — and the honest answer is that both readings have evidence, and that the split is partly ours.
body:
Everything so far has been text. Alchemy is what happens when someone takes the text into a room with a fire in it.

What was actually in the room

Furnaces, glass vessels, sand baths, sealed flasks, and a great deal of patience. The operations are documented and reproducible in outline: distillation, sublimation, calcination, dissolution, coagulation. Substances were purified, combined, heated for weeks, watched for changes of colour. The colour sequence — blackening, whitening, yellowing, reddening — served as the standard map of progress, and it corresponds to observable stages in real chemical processes.

This is the part popular history gets wrong in both directions. Alchemists were not confused mystics staring into fires, and they were not proto-chemists in fancy dress. They were practitioners of a discipline with its own theory, its own apparatus and its own criteria for a job well done. Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton both worked in it seriously, which should end the argument about whether it was intellectually respectable in its own period.

Why the language is impossible

Because it is meant to be. Alchemical writing uses cover names, allegory, contradictory recipes and deliberate omissions — the tradition even has a term for this, Decknamen, cover words. A text may call the same substance the green lion, the dragon, the menstruum and the philosophical mercury within a page.

Three reasons are usually given, and all three are probably true at once: to protect a valuable process from competitors, to keep dangerous knowledge from the unqualified, and because the theory genuinely held that the work resisted plain statement. Whatever the motive, the practical effect is that no alchemical text can be read as a straightforward recipe, and anyone who tells you they have decoded one should be asked how they verified it.

The Great Work

Magnum opus: the full sequence, from raw matter to the philosophers' stone — the agent held to perfect metals and, in many accounts, to heal and extend life. The Emerald Tablet supplied the warrant: separate, refine, raise, return, and the thing comes back carrying the powers of above and below. Read as chemistry, that is a description of reflux distillation. Read as anthropology, it is a description of a person.

The argument that will not close

Nineteenth and twentieth-century writers — Mary Anne Atwood, later Carl Jung — argued that alchemy was always essentially about inner transformation, with the laboratory as symbol. Jung's version, treating alchemical imagery as a projection of psychic processes, has been enormously influential and is how most people meet the subject today.

Historians of science have pushed back hard. Lawrence Principe and William Newman have shown that many texts read as pure allegory describe operations that can be performed, and that the sharp division between “spiritual alchemy” and “chemistry” is largely a nineteenth-century invention projected backwards. Their preferred term, chymistry, marks a field that had not yet split.

Our reading, stated as ours: the evidence is strongest for practitioners who took the material work seriously and understood it within a cosmology in which matter and soul answer each other. That is not the same as saying the furnace was a metaphor. It is saying the two readings were not yet separable — and that the tidy separation people now argue about is a question we brought to the material, not one it was built to answer.

If you keep one thing: the operations were real, the language was deliberately opaque, and the modern spiritual-versus-chemical split is a later question asked of an earlier practice.
facts: Nigredo, albedo, citrinitas, rubedo — blackening to reddening
Decknamen: one substance, many names, on purpose
Newton, Boyle — alchemy was mainstream natural philosophy
Principe & Newman: 'chymistry', a field not yet split
faq: No. Some transmutation demonstrations were fraudulent, others were honest misreadings of real reactions that produced gold-coloured alloys. The absence of success did not discredit the field in its own time, because the theory could always locate the failure in the operator.

Jung was doing psychology, not history, and his readings say more about twentieth-century inner life than about seventeenth-century laboratories. That makes them interesting on their own terms and unreliable as history — a distinction worth keeping when someone quotes him as evidence about what alchemists believed.
Is there anything usable here today?

As method, yes: the insistence on staged work, on watching for change rather than forcing it, on gentleness with great skill. As chemistry, no. Anyone selling alchemical practice as physical medicine is selling something the sources do not support.
sources: Lawrence M. Principe, The Secrets of Alchemy (Chicago UP, 2013) — the standard modern account, including the Decknamen problem.
William R. Newman & Lawrence M. Principe on 'chymistry' and the historiography of the spiritual/chemical split.
